report.answer_text:
On April 2, 2025, President Trump announced a broad set of "reciprocal" tariffs, which he called "Liberation Day."
Legal basis: Trump cited the US trade deficit and the decline in US manufacturing. He invoked the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to issue the executive order.[1] It was Executive Order 14257[2].
Main components
Baseline tariff: A 10% tariff on all imports from all countries, effective April 5.[3]
Country-specific rates: Higher tariffs replaced the 10% baseline for specific countries listed in an annex. These took effect April 9.[3] Examples were 34% on China, 20% on the EU, 46% on Vietnam, 32% on Taiwan and 26% on India.[4] The administration described these as targeting the "worst offenders." In total, about 185 countries were affected.[4]
Autos: 25% tariffs on foreign auto imports took effect the next day, as previously indicated.[4]
Exemptions
Canada and Mexico were exempt from the reciprocal tariffs.[3] They remained subject to the 25% tariffs imposed the month before.[4]
Goods exempted included copper, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, certain critical minerals, and energy products. Steel, aluminum and autos were also exempt because they were already under separate 25% tariffs.[3]
China: The new tariffs were additive. China already faced 20% tariffs, so the 34% reciprocal rate brought it to 54% on most products.[5] China's rate later escalated sharply as the two countries retaliated against each other.
What happened afterward
Within a week, the administration announced a 90-day pause on the country-specific rates. Most countries dropped to the 10% baseline, and China's elevated rates stayed.[6]
Trump ordered the country-specific tariffs to resume on August 7, 2025.[7]
On May 28, 2025, the US Court of International Trade ruled that Trump had overstepped his IEEPA authority and ordered the tariffs vacated.[7] I haven't checked how that litigation was resolved, so check a current source for the tariffs' present legal status.
